name: Risk Assessment Systems
description: Insurance risk assessment systems organize information used to evaluate proposed coverage and support underwriting decisions. Iranian proposal forms illustrate the importance of declared assets and loss histories, while international supervisory guidance provides a framework for examining the accountability of more advanced analytical tools.

seo.title: Insurance Risk Assessment Systems in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore the evidence behind insurance risk assessment in Iran, from proposal forms and loss histories to the governance of analytical systems.

content.heading: Assessment begins with the information collected
content.content:
An insurance risk assessment system supports underwriting: evaluating a proposed risk before deciding whether and on what terms to insure it. The available Iranian evidence offers a concrete starting point in the information requested from applicants, rather than proof of a particular scoring algorithm.

A residential fire-insurance proposal form bearing Dana Insurance's name asks about previous insurance and claims, including the amount and cause of earlier losses. It also separates categories of insured property and requests their values in Iranian rials. These fields distinguish the applicant's insurance history from the assets proposed for coverage. The document is evidence of an information-collection structure; it does not disclose how an insurer weights each answer or calculates a premium. [s1]

Digitizing such a form would therefore establish only part of a risk assessment system. A searchable record of declared values is different from a validated prediction of future losses. Nothing in the inspected form establishes the use of machine learning, automatic acceptance, or a nationally shared underwriting score. Its publication date and current operational status are also unverified. [s1]

content.heading: What advanced analytics can—and cannot—establish
content.content:
International experience helps explain the distinction between collecting data and making an analytical decision. The European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority, or EIOPA, describes supervised machine learning as using previously labelled data to generate predictions or scores. Its discussion identifies pricing, underwriting, fraud detection, and claims management as insurance applications. These are European examples, not evidence that equivalent systems have been deployed in Iran. [s2]

EIOPA also distinguishes tools that assist staff from systems producing outputs that still require human validation. That distinction matters when reading a supplier's description of an 'intelligent' insurance product: the label alone does not reveal who makes the consequential decision. [s2]

The International Association of Insurance Supervisors, or IAIS, published its final application paper on AI supervision in July 2025. Its stated themes include accountability, robustness and security, explainability, and fairness and redress. These provide a useful international framework for questioning a system's design, but do not establish Iranian legal requirements or compliance by an Iranian insurer. [s3]

content.heading: What remains to be demonstrated in Iran
content.content: The evidence supports a limited conclusion: structured underwriting inputs exist, and international supervisors identify governance questions for increasingly analytical insurance systems. A fuller account of Iranian deployment requires insurer documentation identifying the products assessed, the data used, the role of human review, and measured results. Without that evidence, claims that automation has improved pricing accuracy, widened access, or reduced losses would be premature. [s1][s2][s3]

name: Claims Systems
description: Claims systems organize the reporting, assessment, documentation, and settlement of insured losses. Iranian service descriptions illustrate different combinations of online submission, expert review, physical evidence, and payment rather than a single fully automated process.

seo.title: Insurance Claims Systems in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iranian digital claims workflows, including online reporting, expert assessment, supporting documents, and the limits of automation.

content.heading: A digital entrance to a longer process
content.content:
A claim begins when someone reports a loss and seeks compensation under an insurance policy. Moving that report online changes access to the process, but does not by itself establish that assessment and settlement are automatic.

Azki, an Iranian insurance comparison and ordering platform, describes a service covering request registration, loss assessment, and online payment. Its claims page limits participation to eligible policies and participating insurers. For corporate supplementary health insurance, it describes collecting supporting documents and forwarding them to the insurer. This is a coordinated service involving document handling, rather than evidence that every stage occurs without human intervention. [s1]

The platform's homepage gives a more detailed motor-claims sequence: the user identifies the insurance type and their role in the accident, supplies insurer and incident information, and is contacted by an assessment expert. It describes payment following assessment and the injured party's approval. This establishes the advertised workflow, not independently verified payment speed or customer outcomes. [s2]

content.heading: Why physical evidence can remain important
content.content:
A Saman Insurance electronic-equipment policy document hosted by retailer 19kala illustrates another arrangement. Its claims instructions begin with an online form, followed by contact from an assessor. The subsequent steps include attending a designated branch with identification, the damaged device, its packaging and accessories, and the insurance certificate. Assessment and repair documentation then support the claim. [s3]

For repairable damage, the instructions request a formal repair invoice and replaced parts; for a total loss, they request a written technical assessment that the device cannot be repaired. The document also provides a branch-based alternative when online registration fails or internet access is unavailable. These are terms in a specific, undated document, not a statement of current requirements for every Saman policy. [s3]

The example shows why an online form should not be treated as proof of a completely remote claims service. The evidence needed to substantiate a damaged physical object can extend beyond the information entered on a screen. [s3]

content.title: The equipment-claims sequence described in the Saman document
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Policyholder"] -->|"Submits electronic claim form"| B["Online notification"]
  B -->|"Prompts assessor contact"| C["Assessor"]
  C -->|"Directs branch attendance"| D["Branch receives device and documents"]
  D -->|"Refers for technical assessment"| E["Designated technical centre"]
  E -->|"Provides repair or total-loss evidence"| F["Supporting claim documents"]
  F -->|"Submitted for settlement process"| G["Settlement and payment"]
```
content.summary: The arrows describe procedural steps in the inspected equipment-policy document. They do not establish current service availability, automatic approval, or a universal Iranian claims process.

content.heading: What the available evidence cannot measure
content.content: These examples document service designs with different boundaries. They do not provide a comparable measure of how often claims finish remotely, how long completed cases take, or how frequently decisions are disputed. A defensible assessment of system performance would require outcome data alongside the advertised steps. The present evidence therefore supports an explanation of workflows, while leaving nationwide effectiveness unresolved. [s1][s2][s3]

name: Online Insurance Sales
description: Online insurance sales bring product information, comparison, ordering, and issuance support into a digital customer journey. Azki's published descriptions illustrate this model in Iran while showing that online ordering can still involve official information checks and professional review.

seo.title: Online Insurance Sales in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore how Iranian online insurance sales connect comparison, ordering, information checks, and issuance, with clear limits on the available evidence.

content.heading: An online seller and an insurer have different roles
content.content:
For an international reader, the first distinction is between the website used to arrange insurance and the company providing the policy. Azki explicitly states that it is not an insurance company. It presents its service as a way to compare insurers and purchase coverage, while its frequently asked questions describe a platform for insurance information, management, and ordering. [s1][s2]

This makes online sales a distribution subject as well as a software subject. The visible customer journey can combine information about products with assistance in completing an order. A comparison screen is one stage in that journey; policy issuance is another. Azki's descriptions retain a role for professional intermediaries and information checks rather than presenting every purchase as an unattended transaction. [s1][s2]

content.heading: What happens between an order and a policy
content.content:
Azki says its staff check required information against official systems before issuance and contact customers when details are incorrect or inconsistent. It also advertises renewal reminders. These features address different stages of the relationship: establishing usable information for an order and helping an existing customer remember a future renewal. [s1]

The platform's frequently asked questions distinguish the ability to submit requests at any time from published staff response hours. This is a useful qualification to the phrase 'online insurance': continuous access to a form does not necessarily mean continuous human processing. Its FAQ also says that formal professional participants control the processes through which it works with insurers approved by Central Insurance of Iran. That is the platform's description of its arrangements, rather than an independently checked license record. [s2]

content.heading: How to interpret the available evidence
content.content:
The inspected material establishes that a provider publicly describes an online comparison and ordering service with human checks. It does not establish that the platform includes every insurer, that every product can be issued immediately, or that online distribution produces lower total costs. Those conclusions would require evidence beyond the provider's explanation of its own service. [s1][s2]

A fuller account of this branch of Iranian insurance technology also needs current regulatory documentation, verified licensing information, and evidence from multiple distribution channels. This page therefore treats Azki as a documented example rather than a proxy for the whole market. Its practical significance is the connection between a customer-facing digital interface and the professional work behind issuance; the scale and effectiveness of that connection remain research questions. [s1][s2]
